answer:
**A visual adapter must learn how to express image features in a space the language model can use.** If both large pretrained components change rapidly from the first step, the alignment target moves while being learned. Freezing them initially and training the projection can make this first stage more stable. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08485) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12597)

After alignment, selectively unfreeze layers or adapters for instruction tuning, often with smaller learning rates for pretrained weights. Include diverse image-language tasks and language-only evaluation to detect destructive adaptation.

**Verify that the image matters.** Swap in a different image while keeping the question fixed. If the answer barely changes when it should, the system may be exploiting textual priors rather than visual evidence. Test OCR, spatial relations, and counterfactual details directly.

The staged recipe is a useful baseline, not mandatory for every architecture or data scale. Some domains need substantial visual adaptation; others benefit from keeping most weights frozen. A low projection loss can coexist with shortcut learning. Select the training schedule from grounded task quality and retention, not simply successful convergence of the adapter objective.

**Technical details and references.**

Initially freeze the pretrained vision encoder and language model and train the projection/adapter on image–text pairs. This aligns visual features with the language model's input space while limiting early destructive updates. Next, unfreeze selected layers or adapters for instruction tuning, using lower learning rates for pretrained weights and diverse text/vision evaluation. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08485) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12597)

This staged recipe is a useful baseline, not a universal necessity. Data scale, domain shift, and architecture may justify joint training or continued freezing. Check whether the model actually uses the image through counterfactual image swaps and visual grounding tests. Monitor language-only performance, OCR, spatial reasoning, and hallucinations. A low alignment loss can hide shortcut learning from captions or answer priors rather than visual understanding.
